title: Design a Ticket Booking Service
brief: Fans buy seats for concerts. When a popular show goes on sale far more people arrive than there are seats, so buyers wait in a line and are let in one at a time in the order they arrived. A seat can only be sold once: it is held for a few minutes while the buyer pays through an outside processor, and released if they do not.
constraints: Browsing seats must respond within 250 ms
About 4,000 requests per second normally, and a hot on-sale makes the demand to buy several times higher
A seat can never be sold to two people
Buyers are admitted from the waiting line in the order they arrived
Payment goes through an external processor, and a failed or abandoned payment releases the seat
About 4 million seats are on sale across 2,000 events

capabilities.label: Browse events and seats
capabilities.hint: Show events and which seats are still free

capabilities.label: Admit buyers in order
capabilities.hint: Let people through from the waiting line in the order they arrived

capabilities.label: Hold a seat
capabilities.hint: Reserve a seat for a few minutes. Two buyers asking for the same seat at once must not both get it.

capabilities.label: Take payment for held seats
capabilities.hint: Charge the buyer through the processor. A double click must not charge twice.

capabilities.label: Release expired holds
capabilities.hint: Free seats whose hold ran out, about 150 per second

queries.label: Find free seats for an event, in seat order
Hold a seat for the buyer

scenarios.title: Typical day
scenarios.description: Steady browsing and a normal rate of purchases.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Browsing and buying have very different needs. How do you stop a rush of buyers from slowing down people who are just looking?
scenarios.debrief: Browsing is served from a cache, and the booking path only sees the few buyers who proceed.

scenarios.title: A hot on-sale
scenarios.description: Three times the traffic, and holds, payments and the waiting line are several times busier still.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: More people want seats than exist. What limits how fast you let buyers through, and what happens to the rest?
scenarios.debrief: Admit workers batch buyers through at a rate the lock-protected hold service can sustain; the rest wait in the stream.

scenarios.title: Payment processor outage
scenarios.description: The external payment processor stops answering.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Payments cannot go through. What happens to held seats and to buyers who are mid-checkout?
scenarios.debrief: Browsing and the line keep working. Only the final payment step fails, and the hold expires and is released.

scenarios.title: Seat database loses a node
scenarios.description: The database holding seat holds loses a node.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: The seat store loses a node. Can you still guarantee no seat is sold twice?
scenarios.debrief: Losing a database node cuts capacity but the replica keeps holds consistent, and browsing is cache-served.

requirements.text: Browsing meets the latency target at peak
Buyers are admitted through a Stream, in arrival order
Something holds seats, and never to two buyers
Browsing keeps working when the payment processor is down
The design explains how the waiting line stays fair
Every query is answered through a key or an index, never by reading a whole table

rubric: A waiting line (a Stream keyed by event) admits buyers at a rate the booking service can sustain; browsers are not slowed by it.
Holding a seat uses a lock or a conditional write, so two buyers cannot take the same seat, and the throughput cost of that lock is understood.
A hold has an expiry, released by a background job or a TTL, so abandoned checkouts free their seats.
Payment is idempotent and behind a timeout; a processor outage fails checkouts, not browsing.
Browsing is served from a cache so it scales apart from the booking path.

reference.summary: Meter buyers through a waiting line, hold seats with row locks, and keep browsing apart from the booking path.
design: User, then a Load Balancer, then a Web Server (autoscale) running 'Browse events and seats', reading a Cache (95% hit) in front of the Database.

Buyers join a line: the Web Server appends to a Stream asynchronously, Admit Workers (batched) read it in order, then a Hold Service (Row locks) takes the seat and a Payment Service (idempotency keys) charges through a Third-party API set to Payment processor.
tradeoffs: The waiting line meters demand into the booking path, so an on-sale becomes a line instead of an outage.
Row locks stop a seat selling twice but limit how fast holds can be taken, which is exactly what the line protects.
